t: #3864 Minimum Cost to Partition a Binary String — Dyadic Segment Tree DP
o: Splitting is only ever allowed on even-length segments into two equal halves, so every final segment is a dyadic interval: length 2^k, aligned to a multiple of 2^k relative to the whole string. The problem is therefore: cover [0, n) with disjoint dyadic intervals minimizing total cost, where a block with X ones costs flatCost if X = 0 else L * X * encCost. Process lengths 1, 2, 4, ... bottom-up: dp[l] for length L is min(its own cost, dp[left half] + dp[right half]). Example 1 splits down to single chars for cost 6; example 2 stops at length-2 blocks for 12.
k: Repeated halving of even segments means all pieces are aligned power-of-two blocks — a perfect segment-tree structure.
Bottom-up DP over block lengths: dp_L[l] = min(cost(l, L), dp_{L/2}[l] + dp_{L/2}[l + L/2]).
Prefix sums of ones give each block's sensitive count in O(1).

a.n: Approach 1: Level-by-level DP over dyadic blocks
a.i: Compute dp for block length 1 across the string, then length 2 combining adjacent level-1 answers, and so on up to the full length. Each level uses prefix sums for counts, and the split option compares parent cost against children's summed optima.
s: Build prefix sums pre[i] = number of ones in s[0..i).
For L = 1, 2, 4, ..., <= n: for each start l, x = ones in [l, l+L).
base = flatCost if x == 0 else L * x * encCost.
If L > 1, base = min(base, dp_prev[l] + dp_prev[l + L/2]); store as the new dp layer. Answer is dp at L = largest power of two >= n... specifically the layer covering [0, n).
a.t: O(n log n) — sum over levels of n - L + 1 positions, with O(1) work each.
a.sp: O(n) per level kept (two layers at a time).

w: Recognizing the dyadic-alignment consequence of 'only even segments split in half' is the whole problem; after that it is textbook segment-tree DP. Beware overflow: L * X * encCost reaches 1e15, so use 64-bit types in C++/Java (JavaScript doubles are safe up to 2^53). Edge cases: all-zeros string (answer flatCost if n is a power of two alignment allows keeping it whole — the DP handles it), and n = 1. Follow-up: allow arbitrary splits, which becomes a general interval DP.
